   Legislative Context
In 1996, California Voters adopted Proposition 218, the “Right to Vote on Taxes Act” which added Articles
XIII C and XIII D to the California Constitution. Article XIII D imposes certain substantive and procedural
requirements on any agency that wishes to levy special assessments.
Article XIII D imposes four basic substantive requirements on assessments1:

  •  All parcels that will have a special benefit conferred upon them and upon which an assessment will
  be imposed must be identified;
  •  The general benefits must be distinguished from the special benefits conferred on the parcels;
  •  The proportionate special benefit derived by each parcel must be determined in relationship to the
  entirety of the capital improvement, the maintenance and operation expenses of the public
  improvement, or the cost of the property related service being provided; and
  •  The amount assessed to a parcel must not exceed the reasonable cost of the proportional special
  benefit conferred on that parcel and does not include any costs attributable to the general benefit.
Since the initial passage of Proposition 218, several court rulings have helped provide context and direction
on the practical implementation procedures and requirements for levying assessments. Several of the key
concepts from these rulings are summarized below.
GENERAL BENEFIT
Article XIII D requires an agency to separate the general benefits from the special benefits conferred
because only special benefits are assessable.
The Court of Appeal in Golden Hills Neighborhood Assn., Inc. v. City of San Diego (2011) (Golden Hills)2
clarified this concept by stating, “Separation and quantification of general and special benefits must be
accomplished by apportioning the cost of a service or improvement between the two and assessing
property owners only for the portion of the cost representing special benefits.”
The Court of Appeal in Beutz v. County of Riverside (2010) (Beutz)3 quoted from the Legislative Analyst’s
Office pamphlet titled “Understanding Proposition 218” which states an agency must, “estimate the
amount of special benefit landowners would receive from the project or service, as well as the amount of
‘general benefit.’ This step is needed because Proposition 218 allows local government to recoup from
assessments only the proportionate share of cost to provide the special benefit.”
The Court in Beutz furthered this idea stating, “Separating the general from the special benefits of a public
improvement project and estimating the quantity of each in relation to the other is essential if an
assessment is to be limited to the special benefits.”
The Court of Appeal in Silicon Valley Taxpayers' Association Incorporated v. Santa Clara County Open Space
Authority (2008) (SVTA) 4 clarified that general benefits are not restricted to benefits conferred only on
persons and property outside the assessment district but can include benefits both conferred on real

 property located in the district or to the public at large. The “public at large” includes all members of the
public, including those who live, work, and shop within the district, and not simply transient visitors.
BENEFIT-BASED NOT COST-BASED
In Bonander v. Town of Tiburon (2009) (Tiburon)5, the Court of Appeal clarified the idea that assessments
must be apportioned based upon benefit rather than cost. The Court stated, “Proportionate special benefit
is the basis upon which a project’s total assessable costs are apportioned among parcels within an
assessment district.”
The assessment on a particular property cannot be based on the relative cost of the improvements, but
rather the special benefit conferred on such property. The Court in Tiburon also stated, “an assessment
represents the entirety of the cost of the improvement or property-related service, less any amount
attributable to general benefits (which may not be assessed), allocated to individual properties in
proportion to the relative special benefit conferred on the property.”
PUBLIC PROPERTY
Section 4, Subdivision (a) of Article XIII D states, in part, “Parcels within a district that are owned or used by
any agency, the State of California or the United States shall not be exempt from assessment unless the
agency can demonstrate by clear and convincing evidence that those publicly owned parcels in fact receive
no special benefit.” Historically there had been differing opinions about whether this requirement that
publicly owned property should not be exempt actually meant those properties must be assessed.
The Court of Appeal in Manteca Unified School District v. Reclamation District No. 17 et al (2017)
(Manteca)6 clarified this issue by stating, “section 4, subdivision (a) of article XIII D of the California
Constitution unambiguously conditions any continuing benefit assessment exemption on a showing by clear
and convincing evidence of no special benefit.”
IMPRECISION
The Court in Tiburon acknowledged the difficulty of trying to precisely assign and measure special benefit,
stating, “Any attempt to classify special benefits conferred on particular properties and to assign relative
weights to those benefits will necessarily involve some degree of imprecision.”
The Court in Tiburon went on to say that a formula assigning equal weight to different special benefits
“may be a legally justifiable approach to measuring and apportioning special benefits, [but] it is not
necessarily the only valid approach. Whichever approach is taken to measuring and apportioning special
benefits, however, it must be both defensible and consistently applied.”

 3. PLANS AND SPECIFICATIONS
The work and improvements proposed to be undertaken by the City and the cost thereof paid from the
levy of the annual assessment provide special benefit to assessor parcels within the Districts defined in the
Method of Assessment herein. Consistent with the Act, the improvements are generally described as
follows:
  1. The installation, maintenance, and servicing of local streetlight and traffic signal structures in close
  proximity, within approximately 90 feet, to certain lots and parcels which provide a direct special
  benefit to such lots or parcels.
  2. The installation, maintenance, and servicing of peripheral streetlight and traffic signal structures
  which provide a special benefit to all the assessable parcels within the Districts and Annexations
  whether or not such parcels are in close proximity to such lighting.
  3. The installation or construction of public lighting facilities, or the acquisition of any existing
  improvements.
Plans and Specifications for the improvements for the Districts are voluminous and are not bound in this
Engineer’s Report but by this reference are incorporated and made a part of this report. The Plans and
Specifications are on file in the office of the Director of Public Works where they are available for public
inspection.
Article XIII D of the California Constitution defines "maintenance and servicing expenses" as, "the cost of
rent, repair, replacement, rehabilitation, fuel, power, electrical current, care and supervision necessary to
properly operate and maintain a permanent public improvement". The improvement funding includes, but
is not limited to, the removal, repair, replacement or relocation of light standards, poles, bulbs, fixtures
and appurtenances, electrical energy, supplies, engineering and incidental costs relating to the
maintenance and servicing of the local and peripheral lighting and traffic signal improvements benefiting
the parcels within the Districts.
The improvements to be maintained and serviced within the Districts are to be part of the local and
peripheral streetlight and traffic signal system of the City that confers special benefit to the Districts'
parcels. The specific location of both local and peripheral streetlight and traffic signal improvements within
the City can be found on the Streetlight Inventory Maps maintained by the City and on file in the office of
the Director of Public Works where they are available for inspection. The City also maintains a lamp
location list that is a tabulated listing of every street in the Districts by alphabetical order. Included in the
items listed for each lamp are the exact location by street address number and lamp size.
Also included within the City streetlight system are traffic signals and highway safety lights (lights mounted
on traffic signal poles). Traffic signal improvements may include both local and peripheral traffic signals.
Local traffic signals are signals or portions thereof installed within the Districts. Peripheral traffic signals are
portions of traffic signals installed outside of the Districts.
The improvements to be maintained and serviced within the Districts include Southern California Edison-
owned streetlights within the right of way of the local public streets located within the boundaries of the
Districts. These lights are all within close proximity to the parcels within the Districts and have been

 5. METHOD OF APPORTIONMENT
The following section includes an explanation of the benefits to be derived from the installation,
maintenance and servicing of the improvements throughout each District, as well as a description of the
assessment methodology used to apportion the total assessment to properties within each District.
Previous annual Engineer’s Reports were prepared by a different engineer of record and language from
the prior year Engineer’s Report9 has been referenced to describe the Method of Apportionment within
the following section of this report.10
The Districts consist of all assessor parcels within the boundaries as defined by the Assessment Diagram
included with this report and the parcels identified by the Assessor Parcel Numbers listed with the
included levy roll. The parcel list includes all privately and publicly owned parcels with the boundaries. The
method used for apportioning the assessment is based on the proportional special benefits to be derived
by the properties in the Districts over and above general benefits conferred on real property or to the
public at large. The apportionment of special benefit is a two-step process: the first step is to identify the
types of special benefit arising from the improvements, and the second step is to allocate the assessments
to property based on the estimated relative special benefit for each type of property.

  Special Benefit
The improvements are expected to confer certain special benefits to parcels within each District. Pursuant
to the Prior Engineer’s Report, the special benefit conferred to parcel is more fully described as follows:
  In the Districts, the streetlight and traffic signal improvements are installed by the
  developers/owners, subdividers of the land. The continued maintenance is guaranteed
  through the inclusion of the land into a streetlight maintenance district. If the installation
  of the improvements and the guaranteed maintenance did not occur, the individual lots
  would not have originated and could not have been sold to any distinct and separate
  owner. The origination of each distinct and separate lot is a special benefit, which permits
  the construction of a building or structure on the property and the ownership and sale of
  the distinct lot in perpetuity.
  All the lots are established at the same time once the conditions regarding the
  improvements and the continued maintenance are met. As a result, each lot within the
  Districts receives a special and distinct benefit from the improvements and to the same
  degree.
  Over time, the improvements continue to confer a particular and distinct special benefit
  upon parcels within the Districts because of the nature of the improvements. The proper
  maintenance of the streetlights and appurtenant facilities reduces property-related

The SVTA decision clarifies that a special benefit is a service or improvement that provides a direct
advantage to a parcel and that indirect or derivative advantages resulting from the overall public benefits
from a service or improvement are general benefits.
In addition to the special benefits described above (i.e., the origination of each parcel and reduction of
crime) the proximate streetlights clearly make each parcel safer, more visible, more accessible, more
useful, more valuable and more desirable; and this further strengthens the basis of these assessments.11

  General Versus Special Benefit
General benefit is an overall and similar benefit to the public at large resulting from the improvements to
be maintained by the assessments levied. Specific language describing the relationship and proportion of
Special Benefit versus General Benefit from the Prior Engineer’s Report has been included below:
The proceeds from the Districts are used to fund increased levels of maintenance to the Districts’
improvements that serve and benefit the properties in the Districts. In the absence of the Districts, such
improvements would not be properly maintained. Therefore, the Districts’ purpose is to ensure that the
necessary and beneficial public facilities for property in the Districts are properly maintained and repaired
over time. The assessments will ensure that street lighting and associated improvements within and
adjacent to the Districts are functional, well maintained and safe. These public resources directly benefit
the property in the Districts and will confer distinct and special benefits to the properties within the
Districts. Moreover, the absence of the improvements, a condition of development would not be met and
future construction in the Districts could be denied. The creation of individual lots, if any, and the
approval for construction in the Districts, is the overriding clear and distinct special benefit conferred
exclusively on property in the Districts and not enjoyed by other properties outside the Districts.
Therefore, the improvements provide special benefit to property in the Districts over and above the
general benefits conferred to the public at large or properties outside the Districts.
Although the improvements maintained by the services may be available to the general public at large,
the improvements and services are specifically designed, located and created to provide additional and
improved resources for property inside the Districts, and not the public at large. Other properties that are
outside the Districts do not enjoy the unique proximity and other special benefit factors described
previously. These improvements and services are of special benefit to properties located within the
Districts because they provide a direct advantage to properties in the Districts that would not be provided
in the absence of the improvements. Any general benefits to surrounding properties outside of the
Districts, if any there were, are collateral and conferred concomitantly. 12

benefits are solely special, as described above, consideration is made for the suggestion that a portion of
the benefits are general. General benefits cannot be funded by these assessments – the funding must
come from other sources.
The maintenance and servicing of these improvements is also partially funded, directly and indirectly from
other sources including the City, Los Angeles County, and the State of California. This funding comes in the
form of grants, development fees, special programs, and general funds, as well as direct maintenance and
servicing of facilities (e.g. curbs, gutters, streets, drainage systems, etc.). This funding from other sources
more than compensates for general benefits, if any, received by the properties within the Districts.

  Cost of Living Inflator
Annually, the amount of assessments for the Districts may be increased, based upon the Consumer Price
Index, All Urban Consumers, for Los Angeles-Long Beach-Anaheim Area ("CPI"), as determined by the
United States Department of Labor, Bureau of Labor Statistics, or its successor. The Assessment Engineer
shall compute the percentage difference between the CPI for February of the current year and the CPI for
the previous February and shall then adjust the existing assessment by an amount not to exceed such
percentage for the following fiscal year. Should the Bureau of Labor Statistics revise such index or
discontinue the preparation of such index, the Assessment Engineer shall use the revised index or a
comparable system as approved by the City Council for determining fluctuations in the cost of living.
The increase of the assessment for Annexation Nos. 186 & 203 may not exceed 3%.
Alternatively, Assessment Districts Nos. 1, 2, 3, and 4 may use the Southern California Edison and
California Public Utilities Commission (CPUC) approved rates for each light fixture adjustment schedule as
the basis for adjustment of the annual rates. As a result, the assessment may be continued to be levied
annually and may be increased by up to the maximum annual CPI adjustment (or CPUC adjustment for
Assessment Districts Nos. 1, 2, 3, and 4), without any additional assessment ballot proceeding. Further, in
the event that in future years the assessments are levied at a rate less than the maximum authorized
assessment rate, the assessment rate in a subsequent year may be increased up to the maximum
authorized assessment rate without any additional assessment ballot proceeding. 13
For Fiscal Year 2025/26, the maximum authorized assessment rates for the Districts (except Annexation
Nos. 186 & 203) are increased by 3.11%, based on the increase of the February 2024 to February 2025
CPI, for All Urban Consumers in the Los Angeles-Long Beach- Anaheim Area, of 3.11%. The maximum
authorized assessment rates for Annexation Nos. 186 & 203 for Fiscal Year 2025/26 is 3.00%.

every year after their formation or annexation, so long as the public improvements need to be maintained
and improved, and the City requires funding from the assessments for these improvements in each
District. As noted previously, the assessment can continue to be levied annually after the City Council
approves an annually updated Engineer’s Report, budget for the assessment, improvements to be
provided, and other specifics of the assessment. In addition, the City Council must hold an annual public
hearing to continue the assessment.

  Appeals and Interpretation
Any property owner who feels that the assessment levied on the subject property is in error, as a result of
incorrect information being used to apply the foregoing method of assessment, may file a written appeal
with the City of Palmdale Public Works department. Any such appeal is limited to correction of an
assessment during the then current fiscal year or, if before July 1, the upcoming fiscal year. Upon the filing
of any such appeal, the City of Palmdale Public Works Engineer or his or her designee will promptly review
the appeal and any information provided by the property owner. If the City of Palmdale Public Works
Engineer, or her or his designee, finds that the assessment should be modified, the appropriate changes
shall be made to the assessment roll. If any such changes are approved after the assessment roll has been
filed with the County for collection, the City of Palmdale Public Works Engineer or his or her designee is
authorized to refund to the property owner the amount of any approved reduction. Any dispute over the
decision of the City of Palmdale Public Works Engineer or her or his designee shall be referred to the
Director of Public Works of the City of Palmdale, and the decision of the Director of Public Works of the
City of Palmdale shall be final.

RECOMMENDATION

Staff recommend that the City Council:

  1. Approve Agreement No. A-9326 with EcoFert, Inc., for installation of new
  fertigation systems and monthly fertigation system service at various park sites for
  a total not to exceed amount of $528,640 for a term of one year from the Notice to
  Proceed, with two additional one-year options to extend; and,

  2. Authorize the City Manager Pro Tem or his designee to execute Agreement No.
  A-9326 with EcoFert, Inc., including minimal and/or non-substantial changes.

BACKGROUND

City Park Maintenance staff manages 140 acres of irrigated turf, with 60% located at
high-use sports complexes–Domenic Massari, Pelona Vista, and Marie Kerr parks.
These fields support frequent soccer, softball, and multi-purpose activities.

As part of the Parks & Recreation Master Plan, staff conducted a citywide sports turf
assessment, which revealed inadequate past maintenance, turf thinning, high soil
sodium levels, and shallow root systems. These conditions impact turf durability and
player safety.

The assessment recommended installing fertigation systems to improve turf health.
Fertigation delivers nutrients through the irrigation system, allowing for consistent,

efficient application, especially critical for heavily used sports fields. Staff agree that
fertigation is necessary to maintain healthy, safe playing surfaces.

DISCUSSION

On February 25, 2025, the City released Request for Proposal (RFP) No. 25-004-3500
for service of fertigation systems at Domenic Massari, Pelona Vista, and Marie Kerr
Parks. The RFP was shared via PlanetBids and published in the Antelope Valley Press.
A pre-bid walk was held on March 5, 2025, with three vendors attending. EcoFert, Inc.
submitted the only responsive proposal by the March 31, 2025, deadline.

This project includes installing seven app-controlled fertigation systems integrated at the
three parks. EcoFert will also provide monthly service and reporting at these parks and
Sam Yellen Park, with an annual summary on system performance and turf health
supported by soil testing.

EcoFert, Inc. successfully installed the fertigation system at Sam Yellen Park in 2024,
demonstrating reliability and effectiveness. Staff recommends awarding the agreement
to EcoFert, Inc. to expand these services.

$528,640; Sufficient funds for fertigation services are budgeted using Measure AV.

SCOPE OF WORK AND SERVICES
Mandatory Site Visits:
1. CONTRACTORS shall visit each property with City staff and conduct a thorough
assessment of each park, the points of connection, irrigation systems and irrigated
green spaces including turf, shrubs and trees, water quality, soil health, micro-
climate, and park usage to design the fertigation systems. Appendix A - Fertigation
System Installation Site Survey Form must be submitted for each POC.

Design:
1. CONTRACTOR shall design and construct fertigation systems at each point of
connection capable of independent injection rates for primary and secondary
nutrients, wetting agents, other specialty products and isolating fertigation according
to programmable irrigation flow rates. Fertigation systems that offer simple, accurate
calibration, are intuitive, and app-based are preferred.

2. CONTRACTOR shall specify all applicable federal, state, and local codes,
regulations, industry standards and best practices in their proposals. Fertigation
systems shall be designed and installed in full compliance with all applicable codes
and regulations.

3. CONTRACTOR shall submit fertigation system technical drawings, specifications,
product data sheets, material submittals, itemized cost projections, and sample
reports to the City with a proposal for review and evaluation.

Installation:
1. CONTRACTOR shall contact Underground Service Alert (USA - Dig Alert) and
obtain a valid Dig Alert ticket for each point of connection prior to any excavation.
CONTRACTOR shall ensure that all underground utilities are properly marked and
identified in compliance with state and local regulations, and excavation shall not
proceed until all clearances have been received and confirmed.

2. CONTRACTOR shall coordinate on-site, pre-construction meeting with City staff,
provide project schedule with weekly updates, obtain written authorization to proceed
and proactively coordinate required inspections and tapping of mainlines with City
staff.

3. CONTRACTOR shall provide and install all necessary equipment, including but not
limited to:

  Concord - Document ID: generated after first signature  2-17
 a) Secure and lockable, marine-grade aluminum insulated enclosures anchored onto
4-inch thick, rebar-reinforced concrete slabs that extend 24” beyond the enclosure.

b) Ergonomically accessible chemical metering injection pumps with programmable
controllers in lockable control boxes. Fertigation systems that offer simple, accurate
calibration, are intuitive, and app-based are preferred.

c) 2 cross-linked polyethylene (XLPE) tanks, appropriately sized for intended
acreage, set on elevated cradles with spill control provisions for each system to
optimize nutrient delivery, improve efficiency, and prevent clogging, scaling, chemical
interactions, and spills.

d) Injector quills, check valves, master valve relay assemblies, mainline saddles, flow
sensors, isolation ball valves, FEP tubing, FEP fittings, horizontal floats, manway
covers, cooling fans, steel controller pedestals, electrical fittings, conduit, and any
other necessary hardware.

4. CONTRACTOR shall install schedule 80 pvc conduit and wiring from the nearest
available power source, routed underground and through the concrete slab into
fertigation system enclosures in accordance with all applicable codes, regulations,
and standards to ensure proper electrical supply and connections for each fertigation
system. All electrical work must be permitted, performed by licensed professionals,
and inspected as required by municipal code, National Electrical Code (NEC), and
Green Book standard specifications for public works construction, latest edition.

5. CONTRACTOR shall install separate schedule 80 pvc conduits for flow sensor
wiring and injection tubing from inside the fertigation system enclosures, routed
underground through the concrete slab to the irrigation system mainlines at a
minimum depth of 18 inches and comply with all applicable codes and standards. The
conduit shall terminate in reinforced, lockable vaults designed to securely house the
mainline saddles and isolation ball valves while providing ample space for servicing
and maintenance.

6. CONTRACTOR shall install a vandal proof, solar-power supply & deep cell battery
backup for fertigation system at the 30th Street West point of connection at Marie
Kerr Park, where electrical power is not available.

7. CONTRACTOR shall submit itemized invoices per fertigation system installed. The
city may retain 20% of the cost of each installation until punch list items are corrected.

8. Any private or public improvements damaged by the CONTRACTOR while
conducting scheduled work shall be replaced in kind at the CONTRACTOR’S
expense within 5 working days from the date of damage unless otherwise authorized

 by City staff.

MONTHLY SERVICE PROGRAM
1. CONTRACTOR shall implement a monthly service program for fertigation systems
at Domenic Massari Park, Sam Yellen Park, Pelona Vista Park and Marie Kerr Park
that include:

a) Firm and consistent monthly service schedule.
b) On-site consultation with city staff to review system operation, monitor site
response and address any concerns.
c) Servicing and calibration of fertigation systems to ensure optimal functionality,
including 24/7 emergency response, with crew mobilization within 4 hours of work
request.
d) Delivery and loading of amendments and specialty products into system tanks, as
prescribed by authorized city advisors, according to periodic agronomic soil testing, to
correct nutrient imbalances and improve soil health and fertility.

2. CONTRACTOR shall submit monthly service invoices for each site with detailed
service reports to the Parks Superintendent, documenting:

a) Amendments and specialty products added to system tanks each month.
b) Comprehensive fertigation system inspection checklists and findings.
c) All maintenance activities performed, including repairs, calibration and
adjustments.

3. CONTRACTOR shall submit annual executive summary to the City, on a date
determined by the Parks Superintendent, evaluating improvements in agronomic soil
conditions, turf root zone development, canopy health and vitality, supported by data
from agronomic soil and leaf tissue testing and site monitoring. All reports shall be
submitted in a clear and organized format, ensuring transparency and accountability
for ongoing fertigation system management.

4. CONTRACTOR shall warranty all labor and fertigation system components,
providing optimized fertigation system operation as designed for the term of the
monthly service agreement, and any extensions or renewals thereof.

5. Any private or public improvements damaged by the CONTRACTOR while
conducting scheduled work shall be replaced in kind at the CONTRACTOR’S
expense within 5 working days from the date of damage unless otherwise authorized

   EXHIBIT C
  SYSTEM SERVICE SPECIFICATIONS

SYSTEM INSTALLATION AND PROGRAM SERVICE SPECIFICATIONS
Initial Site Analysis
CONTRACTOR shall thoroughly walk a site and obtain client information regarding
maintenance, type of usage and watering schedules. Pictures are taken of the
landscapes, and notes made of all property conditions needing special attention.

Soil Test
Soil samples are taken from the landscapes and sent to an independent lab for testing.
The soil test results help CONTRACTOR to develop the most effective solution for treating
the site.

Property Review
CONTRACTOR shall inspect the property to determine water source, type of system,
irrigation system components, irrigation controller information and general site conditions.
CONTRACTOR shall make notes of any conditions or issues that will potentially affect
the operation of the fertigation system to be installed.

System Install Preparation
Using the information gained from the property analysis, CONTRACTOR shall design and
fully assemble an injection system specifically for the site.

Locate point of connection
The injection system shall be installed at the points of connection.

Determine Power Source
110-volt power should be available within 5 feet of the injection site. If power isn't
available, CONTRACTOR can obtain a proposal from a licensed contractor to run power
from the closest source or install a solar powered system.

Type of Injection System
The proper injector and related hardware is based on a number of factors, including the
condition of the irrigation system, type of water, and the size and use of the property.

Size of Holding Tanks
The size of the holding tanks are determined by the type and amount of the amendments
planned to be applied through the injection system on to the site.

Injection System Installation
CONTRACTOR shall provide all injection system equipment, materials, labor and
hardware. The installation is coordinated with the CITY to assure the most effective start
of the Program. Depending on the complexity of the connection and the type of equipment
needed, the installation can take anywhere from a few hours to several days to complete.
 Equipment
CONTRACTOR shall provide all the specialized equipment necessary for the installation.
This typically includes an injector, tank, and hardware needed to connect with the
irrigation system.

Labor
CONTRACTOR shall utilize specially trained personnel, who can install a properly
operating fertigation injection system.

Electrical
There are a wide variety of electrical needs associated with the proper operation of the
injector system. If there is 110-volt electrical power within 5 feet of the point of connection,
CONTRACTOR shall provide all the necessary electrical hookup. Otherwise,
CONTRACTOR shall advise CITY as to necessary steps to bring sufficient power to the
point of connection or install a solar powered system.

Test at Conclusion
CONTRACTOR shall test the injection system at the conclusion of the installation to
ensure proper operation.

Clean Up
CONTRACTOR shall clean up the installation site to the prior condition.

Life of Program Warranty
CONTRACTOR shall warrant the proper operation of the injector system during the entire
time that the Program is in place for the subject site. This warranty includes repair or
replacement of all hardware, as well as associated labor costs.

Soil Amendments
The choice of soil amendments is primarily based upon the test results, the type of water
and type of use of the property.

Soil Needs
Based on soil test results, the CONTRACTOR shall prescribe a specialized blend of
organic based amendments to achieve healthy, sustainable soils.

Type of Landscape
The types of grass and mix of grass to plants/shrubs will have a large effect on what types
of soil amendments will be applied.

Property Use
A high-use sports field, most particularly for football, soccer, lacrosse and other cleated
sports activities, will require a higher amount and different blend of soil amendments than
a casual use park.
 Type of Water
There are three types of water typically used for landscapes - potable, reclaimed and well.
Reclaimed water is tested to determine what negative effects to landscape and what soil
amendments will be needed for healthy soils.

Water Savings
CONTRACTOR's Program includes organic amendments that reduce the need for
irrigation water. It is expected to see between 10% to 20% of water savings dependent
on the CITY’s historical water usage.

Property Service
CONTRACTOR’s trained personnel shall service the property at least once a month while
the irrigation system is operating.

Monthly Amendment Supply
CONTRACTOR shall provide the appropriate amount of soil amendments based upon
the soil analysis.

Monthly System Review
CONTRACTOR shall visually inspect the injector system to determine whether there are
any malfunctions or irregularities.

Annual Soil Test
At least once a year, CONTRACTOR shall take soil samples for testing by a qualified
third-party lab. The results of the soil test are shared with the client and used to establish
the protocol of soil amendments for the following 12 months.

Annual Property Report
CONTRACTOR shall prepare an Annual Report for each property serviced with the
CONTRACTOR Program. The Annual Report shall include the soil test results, a
summary of both site observations and system operation, as well as the CONTRACTOR's
landscape care recommendations to enhance the health of the property.

RECOMMENDATION

Staff recommend that the City Council:

  1. Adopt Resolution No. CC 2025-042, a Resolution of the City Council of the City of
  Palmdale, approving the application for Local Streets and Roads Funds authorized
  under Article 8 of the Transportation Development; and,

  2. Authorize the City Manager Pro Tem as the City’s authorized signer and designated
  contact person for allocation of Transportation Development Act (TDA) funds for
  street and road improvements.

BACKGROUND

Transportation Development Act (TDA) Article 8 funds are intended to fund unmet transit
needs in areas outside the Los Angeles County Metropolitan Transportation Authority
(Metro) service area, i.e., North Los Angeles County and Santa Catalina Island.
However, if there are no unmet transit needs in these areas that are reasonable to meet,
the Article 8 funds can be used for street and road expenditures.

DISCUSSION

Each year, a public hearing is required to determine if unmet transit needs can be
addressed using Article 8 Transportation Development Act (TDA) funds. The City of
Palmdale meets its transit needs through an agreement with the Antelope Valley Transit
 Report to Mayor and City Council

Authority (AVTA). Therefore, TDA funds will be used for minor street and road
improvements.

Article 8 claims are submitted by Palmdale, other North L.A. County cities, and the County
for areas outside the Metro service area. When using Article 8 funds for streets and roads,
the State Controller’s Gas Tax Guidelines (Sections 100–400) apply.

Metro adopted the FY 2024–25 TDA Article 8 allocations on June 20, 2024. To receive
the funds, the City must submit claim forms and an approved resolution by June 30, 2025.
Staff recommend that the City Council approve Resolution No. CC 2025-042 to apply for
the funds.

FISCAL IMPACT

$10,039,029; Annual allocation of TDA Article 8 revenue for FY 2024-25 is budgeted
and will be used for Street Maintenance and Traffic Signal Operations, GIS Operations,
and local streets and roads projects. The total expenditures/encumbered amounts for
FY 24-25 are $8,647,054 and the remaining funds of $1,391,975 will be placed on
reserve to be used for future streets and roads projects. To ensure that TDA funds are
spent in a timely manner and that interest earned on these funds are accrued, allocated,
and expended consistently with the original allocations, local jurisdictions can claim,
each year, only the funds needed for expenditures charged within the fiscal year.

Los Angeles County Metropolitan Authority (LACMTA) has a policy that all allocation
funds claimed and received must be spent or encumbered through August each year.
Any unencumbered funds remaining in local jurisdictions’ accounts on June 30 of the
fiscal year must be returned to Metro for placement on reserve and future drawdown by
the jurisdiction.

BACKGROUND

On November 5, 2018, the Housing Authority acquired the property located at 513 E.
Avenue Q-4, APN 3008-013-902 (Property), in Focus Neighborhood No. 3, for the
balance of the former Redevelopment Agency loans for the Property. At that time, the
Housing Authority contracted with Newport Pacific Capital Corporation to manage the
Property. The four-unit apartment complex consists of four two-bedroom units, with
carport parking for one space per unit. The Property has been vacant since June 2023.
The Property was acquired in accordance with the Housing Authority’s mission to
increase, improve, and preserve affordable housing in Palmdale. In February 2021,
Victory Outreach - Palmdale expressed interest in leasing, rehabilitating, and operating
the Property due to having shared driveway access, shared trash enclosures, and facing
the 507 Q4 property that Victory Outreach - Palmdale had received approval to lease and
operate.

DISCUSSION

Victory Outreach – Palmdale will lease the property at 513 East Avenue Q4 from the
Housing Authority in its current condition to rehabilitate and manage it as affordable
housing. The four housing units will be rented to very low-income residents who are either
homeless or at risk of becoming homeless, in accordance with California Health & Safety
Code. The property manager who resides at the 507 East Avenue Q4 property will
manage both the 507 and 513 Q4 properties.

housing for households at risk, experiencing, or formerly homeless. One of the approved
programs under the LSF grant is the allocation of $361,145 for affordable housing
expansion, to rehabilitate and operate the 513 East Avenue Q4 property to serve
extremely low to low-income families. Victory Outreach -Palmdale has been identified to
rehabilitate and operate the property under the Measure H LSF Agreement.

  THIS AGREEMENT CONTAINING COVENANTS (this “ACC”), dated as of
______________________, 2025, is entered into by and between the HOUSING AUTHORITY
OF THE CITY OF PALMDALE, a public body corporate and politic (“Authority”), and
VICTORY OUTREACH-PALMDALE, a California nonprofit corporation (“Developer”).

  WHEREAS, Developer is the owner of a leasehold interest in that certain real property (the
“Property”) located in Palmdale, California more particularly described in Exhibit A which is
attached hereto and incorporated herein by this reference, pursuant to the Ground Lease; and

  WHEREAS, for the purpose of providing four units of housing that shall be affordable to
Very Low Income households who are at risk of homelessness or currently unhoused exclusively,
the Parties have entered into an Affordable Housing Agreement dated as of June 3, 2025 (the
“Agreement”), which is incorporated herein by this reference, and any capitalized term that is not
otherwise defined in this ACC shall have the meaning ascribed to such term in the Agreement; and

  WHEREAS, the Agreement contains certain provisions relating to the use of the Property.

  NOW, THEREFORE, FOR GOOD AND VALUABLE CONSIDERATION, THE
RECEIPT AND SUFFICIENCY OF WHICH ARE HEREBY ACKNOWLEDGED, THE
PARTIES COVENANT AND AGREE AS FOLLOWS:

  1.  Developer hereby covenants and agrees on behalf of itself and its successors and
assigns in the Property or any portion thereof or any Improvements thereon or any interest therein
that Developer and such successors and assigns shall rehabilitate the Improvements on the
 Affordable Housing Agreement  Agreement No. A-9241

Property, consisting of a residential apartment building containing four rental units and associated
amenities, in accordance with the Authority Loan Documents and plans approved by City.
Developer hereby covenants and agrees on behalf of itself and its successors and assigns in the
Property or any portion thereof or any Improvements thereon or any interest therein that Developer
and such successors and assigns shall comply with all provisions of the LURA, whether affirmative
or negative in nature, and that Developer, its successors and assigns shall carry out the
rehabilitation, construction, development, and operation of the Improvements on the Property in
compliance with the LURA.

  2.  Maximum Incomes.

  a. Developer covenants and agrees for itself, its successors, its assigns and every
successor in interest to the Property or any part thereof, that Developer, its successors and
assignees shall use the Property exclusively as housing to provide four units of affordable housing
for Very Low Income households who are at risk of homelessness or currently unhoused, subject
to all of the terms and conditions of this ACC. The four two-bedroom units shall be rented as
housing exclusively to Very Low Income households who are at risk of homelessness or currently
unhoused at an Affordable Rent as provided in California Health and Safety Code Section 50053
for very low income households (an “Affordable Rent”).

  b.  For purposes of this ACC, the maximum incomes of eligible tenants shall
be determined on the basis of the income limits for Very Low Income households, adjusted for
household size, in the Los Angeles-Long Beach SMSA, published approximately annually by the
California Department of Housing and Community Development (“HCD”). If HCD discontinues
publishing such income limits, then the term “Very Low Income” shall mean a household income
that does not exceed 50% of the area median income (the “Area Median Income”), adjusted for
household size.

  c.  Household income shall be determined using the income sources set forth
in Section 6914 of Title 25 of the California Code of Regulations. Immediately prior to a
prospective tenant’s occupancy of an affordable unit, Developer shall obtain and maintain on file
an income computation and certification form from such prospective tenant dated immediately
prior to the date of initial occupancy. Developer shall verify that the income information provided
by an applicant is accurate by following all applicable Authority policies and procedures and by
taking one or more of the following steps as a part of the verification process: (i) obtaining two
pay stubs from the most recent pay periods, (ii) obtaining a written verification of income and
employment from applicant’s current employer, (iii) obtaining an income verification form from
the Social Security Administration and/or the California Department of Social Services if the
applicant receives assistance from either agency, (iv) if an applicant is unemployed or did not file
a tax return for the previous calendar year, then obtaining other verification of such applicant’s
income as is reasonably satisfactory or (v) obtaining such other information as may be reasonably
required. Developer shall update the foregoing records annually and provide copies of updated
tenant eligibility records and monthly rental records to Authority for review. Upon review of such
 Affordable Housing Agreement  Agreement No. A-9241
Victory Outreach  Attachment No. 3 – Form of Agreement Containing Covenants
APN: 3008-013-902  Page 3

records, Authority may at its option perform an independent audit of the tenant eligibility records
in order to verify compliance with the income and affordability requirements set forth herein.
Developer shall retain the records described in this Section for a period of five years after the date
each record was created.

  3.  Maximum Rents.

  a.  Rents charged to a tenant shall not exceed rents that are affordable to Very
Low Income households. The maximum rent, including a reasonable utility allowance for utilities
and services (excluding telephone) to be paid by Very Low Income households is set forth below:

  (i)  In the case of a Very Low Income household, the maximum
rent shall be a rent that does not exceed 30% of 50% of the Area Median Income, adjusted for
household size appropriate to the unit.

  (ii)  For purposes of determining Affordable Rent, household
size appropriate to the unit shall mean two persons in the case of a one-bedroom unit and three
persons in the case of a two-bedroom unit.

  b.  This affordability requirement shall continue in effect for the full Term of
this ACC.

  c.  Failure to comply with the affordability requirements of this ACC is an
event of default under the terms of the Authority Loan. Pursuant to the Authority Note evidencing
the Authority Loan, subject to the right to cure, the Authority Loan shall be due and payable
immediately if the housing does not meet the affordability requirements of this ACC.

  d.  Upon request, the Authority Executive Director shall notify Developer of
the maximum rents that may be charged, based on the then-current Area Median Income (not to
exceed an Affordable Rent), and the maximum income of households who are eligible to occupy
the Property. Developer shall submit to Authority for review and approval its initial rent schedule
and utility allowances, 30 days prior to initial rental of the units, and on an annual basis thereafter.
Rental rates may be adjusted, and income determinations performed, annually, at the time of lease
renewal. Developer shall provide tenants not less than 30 days’ prior written notice before
implementing any increase in rents.

  4.  Developer, its successors and assigns shall not charge rents in excess of an
Affordable Rent. If Developer has charged a tenant rent in excess of an Affordable Rent, then
Developer shall immediately reimburse the tenant the amount of overpayment, with interest, from
the date of rental payment, at the highest non-usurious rate of interest permitted by law, within 10
days of such determination. Developer may increase rents not more than once annually, subject
to any applicable rent control ordinance then in effect, but in no event shall rent be greater than
the rent permitted by the adjusted rent limits.

following requirements and are approved by Authority:

  b.  Are reasonably related to program eligibility and the applicants’ ability to
perform the obligations of the lease.

  (i)  The selection of otherwise eligible tenants from a written waiting
list in the chronological order of their application, insofar as is practicable; and

  (ii)  The prompt written notification to any rejected applicant of the
grounds for any rejection;

  d.  Provide first priority in the selection of qualifying occupants to persons
displaced by projects assisted by Authority; and

  e.  Provide information to and otherwise attract eligible qualifying occupants
from all racial, ethnic and gender groups in the housing market area. The Parties shall cooperate
to effectuate this provision during Developer’s initial lease-up of the Property and as vacancies
occur.

  6.  Developer, its successors and assigns shall not refuse to accept for occupancy
otherwise eligible qualifying occupants that are holders of a certificate or voucher under 24 CFR
part 982-Section 8 Tenant-Based Assistance: Unified Rule for Tenant-Based Assistance under the

of a comparable document evidencing participation in a HOME tenant-based rental assistance
program because of the status of the prospective tenant as a holder of such certificate of family
participation, rental voucher or comparable HOME tenant-based assistance document.

in favor of the owner in a lawsuit brought in connection with the lease;

Leasehold Mortgagee for the purpose of implementing the mortgagee-protection provisions

new lender’s lien on Landlord’s interest in the Property to this Lease, which subordination shall
be in a form acceptable to Tenant and the holder of such Senior Leasehold Mortgage.

  Any subordination or attempted subordination of this Lease by Tenant to a mortgage, deed
of trust, encumbrance or other security interest in Landlord’s interest in the Property or any part
thereof shall be void ab initio and shall have no force or effect unless first agreed to in writing by
the holder of a Senior Leasehold Mortgage.

  Where there is a right herein to be exercised by a Leasehold Mortgagee and there exists
more than one Leasehold Mortgage, the right may be exercised in the order of priority of each

  Section 2201 Events of Default

  The following shall constitute an “Event of Default” by Tenant:

  (a)  Subject to Force Majeure Delays and other provisions of this Lease that may modify
the provisions hereof, failure by Tenant to commence or to complete construction of the
Improvements according to the scheduled time periods set forth in the Schedule of Performance,

obligations set forth in this Lease.

or involuntary petition proposing the adjudication of Tenant or any guarantor of Tenant’s
obligations hereunder as bankrupt or insolvent, unless the same is dismissed within 90 days.

  (g)  The appointment of a receiver or trustee for the business or property of Tenant
(except by a Leasehold Mortgagee) or any guarantor of Tenant’s obligations hereunder, unless
such appointment is vacated within 10 days of its entry.

information delivered by Tenant to Landlord is materially false.

Lease and Tenant’s right to possession hereunder and all of Tenant’s right, title and interest
hereunder, in and to the Property and Improvements, shall expire and terminate on such date.

the notice and cure provisions of Section 2202 , the non-defaulting Party, at its option, may, after

herein, any remedy now or hereafter available under state or federal laws, including a proceeding

be deemed exclusive, but shall, wherever possible, be cumulative with all other remedies available

  METHOD OF FINANCING

  This is the Method of Financing attached to the Affordable Housing Agreement (the
“Agreement”) dated as of June 3, 2025, by and between the HOUSING AUTHORITY OF THE
CITY OF PALMDALE, a public body corporate and politic (“Authority”), and VICTORY
OUTREACH-PALMDALE, a California nonprofit corporation (“Developer”), relating to
Developer’s rehabilitation of a four-unit apartment building, to be used exclusively to provide four
residential units to be operated as rental housing that is affordable to Very Low Income households
who are at risk of homelessness or currently unhoused at an Affordable Rent, subject to all of the
terms and conditions of the Authority Loan Documents.

  The Project shall be financed by a combination of the Authority Loan, the City Loan, and
Developer funds, as needed. Developer may utilize other financing sources approved by the
Authority Executive Director, so long as such alternative financing does not result in increased
costs to Authority or City.

  1.  Definitions. Any capitalized term not otherwise defined herein has the meaning
ascribed to such term in the Agreement.

  2.  Total Costs. The Parties estimate that the total Project Costs, including, without
limitation, acquisition and rehabilitation, shall be approximately $941,145. Developer shall be
responsible to provide funds if and as needed to pay for cost overruns and contingencies not funded
by the Authority Loan and City Loan.

  3.  Project Budget. The Parties anticipate that all Project Costs shall be as set forth
in the Project Budget. The Project Budget shall be subject to change from time to time, subject to
the prior written approval of the Authority Executive Director or designee (which approval shall
not be unreasonably withheld) and subject to and conditioned on such further review and approval
by the Authority Board as is needed to satisfy applicable law and Authority policies and
procedures, upon which approval the Project Budget shall be replaced by the approved revised
Project Budget. Developer shall demonstrate, to the satisfaction of the Authority Executive
Director, that all Developer funds shall be available for payment of Project Costs when and as
required by this Method of Financing.

  4.  Authority Loan.

prepayment of the Ground Lease over its term, in the amount of $580,000 (“Lease Prepayment”).

repaid to Authority pursuant to the terms of the Authority Note.

  (b)  In accordance with and subject to the terms and conditions of the Agreement
and this Method of Financing, Authority agrees to make the Authority Loan to Developer, and
Developer agrees to borrow such funds for the payment of Project Costs.

  SCOPE OF WORK

  The Improvements to be rehabilitated consist of a two-story residential apartment building
containing four two-bedroom rental units with one-car carport parking space per unit, and all ancillary
and related improvements for the Property. Rehabilitation shall include, without limitation:

  1.  Replacing air conditioning units;
  2.  Installing new water heaters;
  3.  Repairing walls;
  4.  Installing new flooring;
  5.  Replacing windows and screens;
  6.  Repairing the roof;
  7.  Painting the interior and exterior; and
  8.  Landscaping and installing energy efficient light fixtures.

The plans and specifications of the Project shall be subject to Authority’s approval.

  The rehabilitation shall be carried out in compliance with all applicable permits, building codes
and standards in effect in Palmdale, California. Developer shall be responsible for the costs of
complying with all permit, building codes and standards, and fee requirements of City.

  Upon completion of the rehabilitation, Developer shall use the Property exclusively to provide
four residential units to be operated as rental housing that is affordable to Very Low Income households
who are at risk of homelessness or currently unhoused at an Affordable Rent, subject to all of the terms
and conditions of the Authority Loan Documents.

  This MEASURE H LOAN AGREEMENT (this “Agreement”) is entered into as of June
3, 2025 by and between THE CITY OF PALMDALE, a municipal corporation (“City”), and
VICTORY OUTREACH-PALMDALE, a California nonprofit corporation (“Developer”). City
and Developer (individually, a “Party” and collectively, the “Parties”) hereby agree as follows:

  RECITALS

  A.  Developer has entered into an Affordable Housing Agreement dated as of June 3,
2025 with the HOUSING AUTHORITY OF THE CITY OF PALMDALE, a public body
corporate and politic (“Authority”), as it may be amended or modified from time to time (the
“AHA”).

  B.  The AHA provides for the Authority to lease to Developer certain real property,
including all Improvements thereon, located at 513 East Avenue Q4 in the City of Palmdale,
California, illustrated on the site map attached to this Agreement as Attachment No. 1 and legally
described as set forth in Attachment No. 2 (the “Property”).

  C.  The AHA obligates Developer to rehabilitate four existing two-bedroom residential
units located on the Property resulting in four units of rental housing that are affordable to Very
Low Income households who are at risk of homelessness or currently unhoused exclusively at an
Affordable Rent as more particularly described in the AHA, including the Scope of Work attached
thereto (the “Project”).

  D.  Developer proposes to finance the Project with a loan from the City of Los Angeles
County Measure H Funds (“Measure H Funds”) to perform the rehabilitation work and
Authority’s carry of the prepaid lease payments for the Property, or alternative financing proposed
by Developer and approved by Authority.

  E.  Developer wishes to borrow and City wishes to lend Measure H Funds in the
amount of Three Hundred Sixty-One Thousand One Hundred Forty-Five Dollars ($361,145)
(“City Loan”), which will be used exclusively for payment of rehabilitation costs of the Project.

  F.  City’s making of the City Loan pursuant to this Agreement and the fulfillment
generally of this Agreement are in the vital and best interests of the City, and the health, safety and
welfare of its residents, and in accord with the public purposes and provisions of applicable federal,
state and local laws and requirements.

ARTICLE IV DEFAULTS AND REMEDIES

  Section 401  Defaults - General

  a.  Subject to the extensions of time set forth in Section 502, failure or delay by either
Party to perform any term or provision of this Agreement constitutes a default under this
Agreement. The Party who fails or delays must commence to cure, correct or remedy such failure
or delay and shall complete such cure, correction or remedy with reasonable diligence.

  b.  The injured Party shall give written notice of default to the Party in default,
specifying the default complained of by the injured Party. Failure or delay in giving such notice
shall not constitute a waiver of any default, nor shall it change the time of default. Except as
otherwise expressly provided in this Agreement, any failures or delays by either Party in asserting
any of its rights and remedies as to any default shall not operate as a waiver of any default or of
any such rights or remedies. Delays by either Party in asserting any of its rights and remedies shall
not deprive either Party of its right to institute and maintain any actions or proceedings which it
may deem necessary to protect, assert or enforce any such rights or remedies.

  c.  If a monetary event of default occurs, prior to exercising any remedies hereunder,
the injured Party shall give the party in default written notice of such default. The Party in default
shall have a period of ten (10) calendar days after such notice is received or deemed received
within which to cure the default prior to exercise of remedies by the injured Party.

  d.  If a non-monetary event of default occurs, prior to exercising any remedies
hereunder, the injured Party shall give the party in default notice of such default. If the default is
reasonably capable of being cured within thirty (30) calendar days after such notice is received or
deemed received, the Party in default shall have such period to effect a cure prior to exercise of
remedies by the injured Party. If the default is such that it is not reasonably capable of being cured
within thirty (30) days, and the Party in default (1) initiates corrective action within said period,
and (2) diligently, continually, and in good faith works to effect a cure as soon as possible, then
the Party in default shall have such additional time as is reasonably necessary to cure the default
prior to exercise of any remedies by the injured party, but in no event shall such period exceed
sixty (60) days from the date such notice is received or deemed received. In no event shall the
injured Party be precluded from exercising remedies if its security becomes or is about to become
materially jeopardized by any failure to cure a default.

  Consistent with the Board of Supervisors’ policy to reduce the amount of solid waste

  notify its employees, that they may be eligible for the Federal Earned Income Credit under

  requirements set forth in Internal Revenue Service Notice 1015.

  trustworthiness, as well as quality, fitness, capacity and experience to satisfactorily perform

  debar the contractor from bidding or proposing on, or being awarded, and/or performing
